title: Steve Jobs at D8 (2010): Choosing horses, rejecting Flash, and why privacy means asking in plain English
summary: At D8, Jobs explains how a resource-limited Apple succeeds by betting on rising technologies and dropping dying ones (floppy, serial ports, Flash). He also covers customer-first motivation over market cap, privacy as plain-English consent, and why TV innovation is blocked by go-to-market, not technology.

principles.text: With limited resources, win by carefully choosing which technologies to ride and focus energy on rising ones.
principles.quote: the way we've succeeded is by choosing what horses to ride really carefully, technically. We try to look for these technical vectors that that have a future.

principles.text: Technologies have life cycles; back those in spring, not the ones headed for the graveyard.
principles.quote: they have their their springs and summers and autumns and then they you know, go to the graveyard of technology. And so we try to pick things that are in their springs.

principles.text: Great products come from deliberate trade-offs: leave things out and take the heat to serve customers.
principles.quote: we have the at least the courage of our convictions to say we don't think this is part of what makes a great product. We're going to leave it out.

principles.text: Customers pay you to make choices for them; the market will judge, so stay focused on the best product.
principles.quote: They're paying us to make those choices. That's what a lot of customers pay us to do is to try to make the best products we can.

principles.text: Intrinsic motivation outweighs market cap: delighting customers is what gets you to work.
principles.quote: There's nothing that makes my day more than getting an email from some random person in the universe who just bought an iPad over in the UK

principles.text: Privacy means informed consent in plain English, asked repeatedly.
principles.quote: Privacy means people know what they're signing up for in plain English and repeatedly.
